annotations.text: Round one asked what ground the rows stand on. Chris passed on it: the icons themselves are the primitive part, so the marks page is where round two lives. These boards stay as the record of the framings tried.

As shipped. A row is its mark and the counts are loose dots. Nothing says the four rows are one instrument, nothing under them says where the corner begins, and a spent charge is a hollow dot three points across. The marks are not the problem: they took several rounds of care already and no board here redraws them.

A - The rail. One spine out of a chamfered foot in the corner, and every row visibly hangs off it: a nub per row reaching to where its mark begins, a tick per row seam, the top fading out past the last row. Counts become chamfered magazine cells, so a spent charge keeps its outline and the row never changes width. The rounds read as leaving a rack rather than floating. The cheapest direction to build (a dozen segments and the cells) and the most house: this HUD already speaks in hairline rules and chamfers. Cost: the spine is chrome that says nothing on its own, and on a bare kit two rows wear a fair amount of rail (board beside).
The rail on a fresh spawn, which is most of the corner's life: two plain rows, no charges yet. The spine keeps the corner reading as one instrument even when the kit is empty.

B - Bays. A chamfered lip per row, the bracket the radar and the expanded map already wear, and one hairline deck under the block. Each weapon sits in its own bay, which answers where a row begins better than a shared spine can, and gives hover an obvious hit shape. Cells for counts as on A. Cost: five brackets where the rail spends one line, and a lip this small flirts with reading as a parenthesis.

C - The hull plan. The corner is your ship, drawn faint in panel ink, and each mark hangs off the hardpoint that fires it by a hairline leader: the gun at the nose because that is where it is, the bomb in the keel, charges racked off the wing. The most fiction of the five and the best answer to what this corner is about, the machine you are flying. The costs are real: twice the height of the stack, a hardpoint table per hull, and the leaders put ink between you and the counts.

D - The fire arc. A quarter instrument swung out of the corner itself: two arcs, ticks every ten degrees, a station per row, the dial corner answered from diagonally opposite. The most cockpit of the five. Cost: a curved layout for row-shaped content. Hover cards, row order and the direction the block grows in all get harder, and it spends the most screen on the same four facts.

E - Live fire. The shipped geometry, unmoved, but the corner answers the one question a fight actually asks it: can I press this now. A fired trigger recoils with a flash and goes dim, then the barrel relights from the tail as the cooldown runs out, so the line itself is the gauge. A ready row breathes on the clock DEPLOY and ON AIR already breathe on. The last charge pulses. fire_cooldown already sits in sim_ship (sim.h), so this costs one small core getter plus draw code, and it composes with any direction rather than competing with it. The strip along the top is one row's life drawn out flat.

Round two, per Chris: the icons themselves should look cooler, and the counts should be the ship page's circles. So every board counts charges in pages.dot's grammar, solid a charge held, a ring where a spent one was, and proposes a vocabulary for the four drawings. The strip along the top of each board is inspection size; the corner at the lower left is the truth, drawn at the stack's own scale. The marks stay shared with the touch pads, so whichever vocabulary wins is also what a thumb presses on a phone.

As shipped, close up: a line with a dot, a ringed dot, two rings, a rosette. All the care went into the dress (the fan, the rings, the fuse field, the ticks) while the rounds themselves stayed primitives. The gold count dots beside the charges are the pips this round retires.

F - Tracer. The icon is the round the arena fires, frozen: the layered streak with a hot head that a bolt wears in flight (world.weapons' three passes and the halo), the hot core in a ring for the bomb. Nothing to learn, you have watched these cross the screen since your first fight, and in the corner they would draw into the glow layer and breathe on the arena's own pulse. Costs: a gun that is mostly light thins to its head at row size, so the bounce rings end up louder than the round; and a mark made of glow leans on bloom staying on.

G - Ordnance. Rounds built the way hulls are: thin outline over a darker fill, lit at the leading edge. The gun round is a finned dart with a hot core, the bomb a cased shell with four lugs and a lit rim, the repel a shockwave standing off a point, the burst a ring of darts. It reads at any size because it is drawn rather than lit, and the fan becomes a volley of three darts. Costs: the most new geometry of the three, and a dart is a shape to learn where the streak was a fact you already knew.

H - Ordnance, lit. G's bodies under F's light: each dart rides a short fading wake with a halo on its nose, the shell sits in its own glow, the charges radiate. This is what the arena already does to everything it cares about, a body with light coming off it. The likely winner if the brief is simply cooler: it keeps G's legibility at row size and F's heat. Cost: G's geometry plus a glow pass.
